_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-04.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed.

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.

Strong's tags are also taken off any kept place whose tags light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, or whose roots light more words of the verse than there are tags, or, on a question or parallel lines, that were chosen for marked words since changed: such tags are a stretch of words, or name words no longer marked.
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").

places.words_why: "to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name" sets "His name" beside "Him", so the name plainly stands for the person; the verb "believed in" is not part of the figure.
In "takes away the sin of the world" the sin is that of the world's people, so "the world" is put for its people; "sin of" is not part of the figure.

places.why: "My hour has not yet come" uses "hour" in its ordinary sense of a set time. The verse does not plainly put one thing's name for another, and saying what the hour is would need a commentary.

places.words_why: "many people saw the signs He was doing and believed in His name": "His name" plainly stands for Jesus Himself; mark only the name, not the verb.

The verse sets "Whoever believes in Him" beside "he has not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son", so the name plainly stands for the Son. Only "the name" carries the figure, without the verb "believed in".
In "this man truly is the Savior of the world" the ones saved are the world's people, so "the world" is put for its people; "Savior of" is not the figure.

places.why: "It is written in the Prophets" uses a set name for a part of Scripture; a reader takes it in its ordinary sense, not as a figure.

places.words_why: "which I will give for the life of the world" means the life of the world's people, so "the world" is put for its people; "life of" is not the figure.
"no one who wants to be known publicly ... show Yourself to the world": the world here is plainly the people who would see Him; the verb is not part of the figure.

places.why: "because His hour had not yet come" means His set time had not come. "Hour" has its plain sense here, so no metonymy is plain at these words.
"because His hour had not yet come" uses "hour" for an appointed time, its ordinary sense. No word is plainly named for another thing it goes with.

places.words_why: In "what I have heard from Him, I tell the world" the world is plainly its people, who are told; "I tell" is not the figure.

places.why: "No one can snatch them out of My hand": the hand plainly stands for His keeping and power, and 10:29's "My Father's hand" confirms it. The figure is carried by "My hand", not by the verb before it.

"Look how the whole world has gone after Him!": only people follow someone, and 12:18 names the crowd, so "the world" plainly stands for its people. The figure is "the whole world"; the verb is not part of it.
"The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" names the time itself, in the ordinary sense. No metonymy is plain.

In "Father, glorify Your name!" and the answer "I have glorified it", the word "name" can be read in its ordinary sense of renown. Nothing in the verse sets the name beside the Father Himself the way John 3:18 does, so a reader would need a commentary to see the name standing for the person. In doubt, it does not go live.

"the prince of this world will be cast out" reads plainly as the ruler of a realm. The verse does not plainly show "world" named for something else at these words, and the title needs a commentary to explain it.

places.words_why: "I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world" follows "I do not judge him", so the world is plainly its people; mark "the world", not the verb.

places.why: "His hour had come to leave this world": the verse itself says what the hour is, the time to leave. So "hour" has its plain sense of a set time and is not named for something else.

"the Father had delivered all things into His hands": all things cannot lie in physical hands, so "His hands" plainly stands for His power and authority. The figure is "His hands", not the whole clause.
"the world will see Me no more, but you will see Me": only people see, and "the world" is set against "you", so it plainly stands for people. The figure is "the world", not the whole clause.

places.words_why: "reveal Yourself to us and not to the world" sets the world beside "us" as people; mark "the world" without "not to".

places.why: "the prince of this world is coming" is said plainly as the ruler of a realm. No word is plainly put for another at these words.
"If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first": only people hate, so "the world" plainly stands for its people. The figure is "the world", without the "If" and the verb.

places.words_why: "the world hates you" and "it would love you as its own" plainly put "the world" for its people; mark "the world" without the verb.
"He will convict the world in regard to sin", explained in 16:9 as "because they do not believe in Me", plainly puts the world for its people; the verb is not the figure.

places.why: "because the prince of this world has been condemned" is a title for a ruler of a realm, said in plain terms. No metonymy is plain at these words.

places.words_why: "you will weep and wail while the world rejoices": rejoicing is done by people, so "the world" is put for its people; mark it without the verb.

places.why: "Father, the hour has come" uses "hour" for the appointed time, in its ordinary sense. Nothing in the verse plainly names one thing for another.

places.words_why: "I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me" sets the world beside people, so it is plainly put for its people; "on behalf of" is not the figure.
"the world has hated them": hating is done by people, so "the world" is put for its people; mark it without the verb.
"so that the world may believe that You sent Me": believing is done by people, so "the world" is plainly put for its people; mark it without the verb.
"so that the world may know that You sent Me": knowing is done by people, so "the world" is plainly put for its people; mark it without the verb.
"although the world has not known You, I know You, and they know" sets the world beside persons, so it is plainly put for its people; mark it without the verb.
In "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" no one drinks a cup itself, so "the cup" is plainly put for what it holds; mark the cup, not the verb.
"I have spoken openly to the world ... where all the Jews come together" plainly puts the world for the people He spoke to; mark it without the verb.

places.why: "unable to eat the Passover" uses the word in its ordinary sense of the Passover meal or lamb; a reader would not see a figure there without being told.
"declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues" uses "tongues" in its ordinary sense of languages, a set use the task names as one to drop.
"the great and glorious Day of the Lord" names an appointed time. The verse does not plainly put one thing for another at these words.
"calls on the name of the Lord" can be read literally as calling on the Lord by His name. The verse does not force "name" to stand for the person, and when in doubt the place stays out.
The verse sets "Salvation exists in no one else" beside "no other name", so "name" plainly stands for the person. Only "no other name" carries the figure. "under heaven" does not.
places.words_why: "Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name" sets "name" beside "no one", so the name plainly stands for the person; "no other" is not the figure.

places.why: In "hanging Him on a tree" the Greek word means wood, so hanging on wood is a literal description. The verse itself does not plainly show one thing named for another.
"suffering disgrace for the Name", after 5:40 "the name of Jesus", plainly means for Jesus Himself: a name for the person. Only "the Name" carries it.
"O house of Israel" is a set name for the nation, read in its ordinary sense; a reader would not see a figure in it without being told.
"Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them": "them" shows the region stands for its people. Only "Samaria" carries the figure.
"I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting" is the Lord saying that persecuting His people is persecuting Him. No name is put for another at these words, and no live form plainly fits.
"all who call on Your name" can be read literally as calling on the Lord by name. The verse does not plainly make "name" stand for the person, so when in doubt it stays out (as with Acts 2:21).
"how much he must suffer for My name" means suffering for Christ Himself (9:15 "carry My name"): a name for the person. Only "My name" carries it.
Same as Acts 5:30. The Greek word behind "tree" means wood, so hanging Him on wood is literal. The verse does not plainly show a figure at these words.
The BSB's "circumcised believers" is literal wording. It describes believers who were circumcised, and nothing in it is named for something else.
"speaking in tongues" is a set name for a gift. A reader would not see a figure in it without being told.
"the circumcised believers took issue with him" is literal wording in the BSB. The abstract-for-concrete figure is only in the Greek and is not shown by these words.
"to turn the proconsul from the faith" can simply mean turning him from believing (he believes in 13:12). It is not plain that faith is put for the message believed.
"the reading from the Law and the Prophets" uses a set name for a section of Scripture, not a plain figure.
"nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word": a city cannot gather or hear, its people do. Only "the whole city" carries the figure.
"Moses ... is read in the synagogues on every Sabbath": a man is not read aloud, so Moses plainly stands for the law he wrote. Only "Moses" carries it.
The plain figure in the mob's cry "These men who have turned the world upside down" is overstatement about a few men's visits, which is hyperbole, not metonymy. The marked words carry the hyperbole.
"Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it": no literal blood is meant, and "innocent of it" shows blood stands for the guilt of their ruin. "Your blood" carries it.
A province and the world cannot worship; their people do, so the places plainly stand for their people. "worshiped by" is not part of the figure.
places.words_why: In "worshiped by all the province of Asia and the whole world", the places stand for their people. Mark the two place phrases and leave out the joining "and".

places.why: "the whole city was in disarray. They rushed together": "They" shows the city means its people. The span should end at "the whole city", not on "was".
Paul shed no blood. 20:27 shows he means he bears no guilt for their ruin, so "blood" stands for death and its guilt. The span should be "the blood of all men".
"which He purchased with His own blood" can be read of the actual blood Christ shed. It is not plain that "blood" is only put for His death, so when in doubt it stays out.

"to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or observe our customs", with 21:20 "zealous for the law": Moses plainly stands for the law given through him. Only "Moses" carries it.
"The whole city was stirred up, and the people rushed together": the city plainly stands for its people. The span should end at "The whole city", not on "was".

"all Jerusalem was in turmoil" follows "The whole city was stirred up, and the people rushed together" (21:30), so the city plainly stands for its people. The marked span "all Jerusalem was in" breaks off mid-phrase. Only "all Jerusalem" carries the figure.

In "why do you persecute Me?" the Lord counts the persecution of His people as against Himself. No word is put in place of another, so the verse does not plainly show metonymy or any other live form at these words.
"I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting" is the same statement as 22:7. No one thing is named for another, so no live form is plainly shown at these words.
"written in the Prophets" uses a set name for a section of Scripture, not a plain figure.

"why do you persecute Me?" is the same as 22:7: Christ counts His people's suffering as His own. That is not one thing named for another. ("kick against the goads" in the same verse is not what is marked.)
"I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting" puts no name in place of another, so the verse does not plainly show metonymy at these words.
"from the Law of Moses and the Prophets" uses a set name for sections of Scripture, not a plain figure.

In the Greek, "hē akrobustia ... phulassē" ("the uncircumcision keeps") does put uncircumcision for the uncircumcised man. But the tags also mark G1345 dikaiōmata "requirements", which has nothing to do with the figure, and G0203 also hits the second, literal akrobustia ("his uncircumcision"). The tags cannot be narrowed here, and stripping them would leave the BSB words "a man who is not circumcised", which show no figure in English. So the place cannot go live correctly. The same figure is kept at 2:27.
The BSB's "The one who is physically uncircumcised" is literal and names a person directly. The figure is only in the Greek, and the marked words do not show it.

"how could God judge the world?" follows God's "wrath on us" (3:5), so what is judged is plainly the world's people: the world put for those who live in it. Only "the world" carries the figure, not "judge".

"every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God": only people can be held accountable, and the phrase stands beside "every mouth", so the world plainly stands for its people. The span is narrowed to "the whole world".

In "as attested by the Law and the Prophets", the prophets themselves bore witness, so "the Prophets" may mean the men and not their books. Unlike "written in the Prophets" (Acts 24:14) or persuading "from" them (Acts 28:23), nothing in this verse plainly shows a name put for something else. In doubt, it does not go live.

places.words_why: In "the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood", blood stands for His sacrificial death. Mark the noun phrase without "in".

places.why: The Greek "on the circumcision or also on the uncircumcision" plainly names the two peoples by their sign, but the tags cannot stand. They list G1909 and G3588 twice, which the build refuses, and the article tag also lights up the unrelated "the" before "blessing", "Abraham" and "faith". Without the tags, the BSB's "the circumcised" shows no figure, so nothing at the marked whole verse shows it. It could come back tagged only G4061 and G0203.

places.words_why: In "justified by His blood", blood stands for His death, as the next verse's "through the death of His Son" shows. Mark the noun phrase without "by".

places.why: In the list of hardships, "sword" is the one tool rather than a condition, so it plainly stands for violent death by the sword, and 8:36 confirms it with "we face death all day long ... sheep to be slaughtered". "famine or nakedness or danger" are literal, so the mark narrows to "sword".

places.words_why: In "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord", the name stands for the Lord Himself, as the verse before's "all who call on Him" shows. Mark the name phrase, not the verb.

places.why: "riches for the world" is answered at once by "riches for the Gentiles", which plainly shows that the world stands for its peoples. The word carrying the figure is "the world", not "riches", so the mark narrows to it.

In "the reconciliation of the world", only people can be reconciled, so the world plainly stands for its people, set against Israel's rejection. The figure is carried by "the world", so the mark narrows to it.

"every knee will bow before Me; every tongue will confess to God" plainly names a part of the body for the whole person (every person will bow and confess). That is a part for the whole, as both readers proposed, not metonymy. It is marked on "every knee" and "every tongue".
The whole verse is marked, and the BSB's "with one mind and one voice" reads as a plain idiom for unity. A reader would not plainly see one thing named for another without being told.

The Greek "a servant of circumcision" plainly names the Jewish people by the rite, but one of the two tags is G1096, "to have become", which has nothing to do with the figure. Without the tags, the BSB's "the circumcised" shows no figure at the marked whole verse. It could come back tagged only G4061.
"the message of the cross" reads naturally as the message about the crucifixion. The figure is too faint to be plain without a commentary.

"saved on the Day of the Lord" uses the fixed name for the time of the Lord's coming. Nothing in the verse shows that "day" is put for something else, so a reader would not see a figure without being told.

places.words_why: In "the saints will judge the world", the world stands for its people. Mark "the world" without the verb "judge".

places.why: "Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ?" has no drinking verb, so the cup can be read as the vessel used in the meal. A reader would need a commentary to see the container put for its contents here.

places.words_why: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too": nobody drinks a cup, so the cup is plainly put for what is in it. The figure is in the cups, not in the verb "drink".
"eat this bread and drink this cup": the cup is plainly put for its contents. Only "this cup" carries the figure, not the verb.
"drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner": the cup is plainly put for what is drunk from it. Mark the cup, not the verb.

places.why: "eats of the bread and drinks of the cup" means drinking from the cup, which is literal. Unlike 11:27's "drinks the cup", nothing here names the cup in place of what it holds.
"to another speaking in various tongues" is the set name of a gift, and "tongues" for languages is an ordinary English sense. A reader would not see a figure here without being told.
"Do all speak in tongues?" uses the set name of the gift. "Tongues" in its ordinary sense of languages is not plainly a figure.
"If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels" uses "tongues" in its ordinary sense of languages, the same set expression as speaking in tongues. No plain figure for a reader.
"he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men" is the set name for the gift. It is not a figure a reader would see unaided.
"The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself" is the set name of the gift, with "tongue" in its ordinary sense.
"I wish that all of you could speak in tongues" is the set name of the gift, not a figure plain in the words.
"if I come to you speaking in tongues" is the set expression for the gift. A reader would not see a figure there.
"the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret" is the set name for the gift, with "tongue" meaning language in its ordinary sense.
"I speak in tongues more than all of you" is the set name of the gift, not a plain figure.
"ten thousand words in a tongue" uses "tongue" in its ordinary sense of a language. A reader would see no figure here.
In "By strange tongues and foreign lips" the marked "strange tongues" is "tongues" in its ordinary English sense of languages. It does not plainly show one thing named for another.
"everyone speaks in tongues" is the set name of the gift, not a figure a reader would see without being told.
"everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue" uses "a tongue" as the set name of the gift in a list of gifts. No plain figure.
"If anyone speaks in a tongue" is the set name of the gift, not a plain figure.
"do not forbid speaking in tongues" is the set name of the gift, with "tongues" in its ordinary sense.

places.words_why: "God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men's trespasses against them": the world is plainly put for its people, since "them" refers to men. Only "the world" carries the figure, not the verb.

places.why: The whole verse is marked, and the BSB's "by the testimony of two or three witnesses" has no figure in English. Mouth for testimony is only in the Greek, and three of the four tags point at words that do not carry it: epi, two and witnesses. A trim to BSB words would lose the Greek and show nothing.

The Greek "the gospel of the uncircumcision ... of the circumcision" plainly names Gentiles and Jews by the sign. But the tags mark G2098, "gospel", and every article, which do not carry the figure, and they leave out G4061, "circumcision", which does. Without the tags, the BSB's "the uncircumcised" and "the circumcised" show no figure. It could come back tagged G0203 and G4061.

The Greek "apostleship of the circumcision", set against "the Gentiles", plainly names the Jews by the sign. But the tags mark G0651, "apostleship", and the article G3588, which also lights up the unrelated "the [One]" and the "the" before "Gentiles". Without the tags, the BSB's "the circumcised" shows no figure. It could come back tagged only G4061.

places.words_why: "if I am still preaching circumcision ... the offense of the cross has been abolished": the cross is plainly put for the preaching of Christ crucified, not the wood. Mark "the cross" alone.

places.why: No one boasts in a piece of wood, and "through which the world has been crucified to me" shows the cross standing for Christ's crucifixion and its work. The figure is plain, but the marked words take in "boast, except in" and cut off "of our Lord Jesus Christ".

"Redemption through His blood" still makes sense taken literally, as His blood truly shed in sacrifice. Reading "blood" as a name for His death is a reading the verse allows but does not show, so in doubt it stays out.

"called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision" plainly names Gentiles and Jews by the rite, and the BSB shows it in English. The whole verse was marked, and the tags fall twice on λέγω ("being named") and miss περιτομῆς, so the tags go.
places.words_why: "called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision": the rite plainly names the circumcised people who do the calling, so the figure is plain. It sits in "circumcision". "the so-called" is Paul's qualifier and carries no part of it, and "the circumcision" is not one unbroken piece of the verse.

places.why: "Brought near through the blood of Christ" reads naturally as His shed blood. That "blood" here names something else, His death, is not plain from the words, so in doubt it stays out.

"You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord" says the readers were darkness and are light, outright. That is plainly a metaphor, not one thing named for another it goes with. The marked words should take in both halves.
places.words_why: "you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord" plainly says the people are darkness and light. The two "you are" statements carry the metaphor; "but now" and "in the Lord" are not needed.

places.why: In "for the faith of the gospel", "the faith" is the ordinary word for what is believed, and a reader would not see a figure there without being told. The span also takes in "contending side by side", a different picture.

"It is we who are the circumcision" plainly names God's people by the rite, and the BSB shows it in English. The whole verse was marked, and the tags take in ἐσμεν ("are") and every article, including οἱ ("those") of the next clause, so the tags go.

places.words_why: "Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ": nobody is an enemy of the wood, so the cross is plainly named for Christ crucified and His message. The figure is in "the cross of Christ", not in "enemies".

places.why: In "making peace through the blood of His cross" the blood was literally shed on the cross, so "His cross" is not named for something else. Reading "blood" as put for His death is a figure only some would see.

"When Christ, who is your life, appears": the verse before says "your life is now hidden with Christ in God", and many readers take "Christ ... is your life" as a plain statement about Christ himself (compare "I am the life"), not as life named for its source. Whether this is metonymy, metaphor or a literal claim is a matter of reading, so with no writer named it does not go live.

"The wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience" reads as God's own wrath coming on them. That "wrath" stands for its punishment is a reading the words allow, not one they force, so in doubt it stays out.

The figure lies in the Greek nouns περιτομὴ καὶ ἀκροβυστία, but the tags also hit Ἰουδαῖος ("Jew") and all three καί, so they cannot stand. Without them, the BSB's "circumcised or uncircumcised" only describes people as they are, and no figure shows in the English.

The BSB's "These are the only Jews among my fellow workers" uses "Jews" literally. The figure is only in the Greek "of [the] circumcision", and the tags include the preposition ek, which does not carry it. Stripping the tags would leave a literal word lit.
"Our deliverer from the coming wrath" reads as God's wrath itself coming. That "wrath" is named for its punishment is not plain from the words, so in doubt it stays out.

"Who is our hope, our joy ... if it is not you yourselves", with 2:20 "You are indeed our glory and our joy", plainly names the people for the hope and joy they give. But the span "who is our hope" takes in the question words and leaves out "our joy".

"The Day of the Lord" is a fixed name for the event, and nothing in the verse shows one thing named for another. The plain figure in the verse is the likeness "like a thief in the night", which is not at these words.
"God has not appointed us to suffer wrath" reads as suffering God's wrath itself, so the figure is not plain. The span also takes in "appointed us to suffer".

places.words_why: In "Christ Jesus our hope" a person is plainly named by the hope He gives, so the figure is clear. But the word that carries it is "our hope", not the name of Christ Jesus.

places.why: In "hold to the mystery of the faith", "the faith" is the ordinary word for what Christians believe, and a reader sees no figure there without a commentary.
In "he has denied the faith", "the faith" is the ordinary word for the Christian belief. The verse does not plainly show one thing named for another.
In "wandered away from the faith", "the faith" is the ordinary word for the body of belief, so there is no plain figure. The span also takes in "wandered away", a separate picture.
In "swerved away from the faith", "the faith" is used in its ordinary sense of the Christian belief, so there is no plain figure. The span also takes in "swerved away".
In "disqualified from the faith", "the faith" is simply the Christian belief, and a reader would not see a figure there without being told.
"those of the circumcision" is a set name for a party. A reader takes it as a name, not as a figure. The tags also point at articles and "ek".
"So that they will be sound in the faith" may mean their own believing or the teaching believed. Either way no figure plainly shows at these words.
"with the house of Israel" is the set name for the nation. A reader takes it as a name and would not see "house" as a figure without being told.
"with the house of Israel" is the set name for the people. It reads as a name, not as a figure plain in the words.

"Not by the blood of goats and calves, but by His own blood" keeps to the high priest's rite, where blood is blood. A figure naming His death by "blood" is not plain from the words, so in doubt it stays out.
"The blood of Christ" answers 9:13's "blood of goats and bulls" within the same sacrifice picture, where blood is sacrificial blood. A separate figure at that word is not plain.
"Offered once to bear the sins of many" reads as bearing the sins themselves. Taking "sins" as their penalty needs a commentary, so the figure is not plain.
"Confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus" keeps to the high priest's rite, where blood is blood. A figure at "blood" is not plain, so in doubt it stays out.

Right after "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay", "to fall into the hands of the living God" plainly uses hands for God's power to judge. Since the hands are said of God, the closer form is human parts said of God. The marked words should be the hands said of God, not the verb phrase "fall into the hands of".

places.words_why: "The world was not worthy of them" plainly puts the world for its people. Only "The world" carries the figure, not "was not worthy".

places.why: "By His own blood" answers v.11's "blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin". Inside that sacrifice picture the blood is the blood offered, and Jesus did shed blood. So the verse does not plainly name blood for something else, such as His death. Too doubtful to go live unsourced.

In "sprinkling by His blood", the blood is the thing sprinkled, in a picture taken from the old covenant rite. The figure a reader sees is that picture, not "blood" named for another thing, so the metonymy at "by His blood" is not plain.

"the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish" can be read as the lamb's literal sacrificial blood. Taking "blood" as named for His death is a reading the verse does not force, and the readers split, so it stays out. "precious" carries no figure.

"the Day of the Lord" is a fixed name for the time of judgment, not one thing plainly named for another. The plain figure is the simile "like a thief", and 2-peter-3-10-simile-seen already marks it, so this place is not changed into a simile.

"the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin" is sacrifice language where blood is the cleansing agent. That "blood" is named for His death is an interpretation, not plain in the words, so when in doubt it stays out.
In "if the world hates you", only people can hate, so "the world" plainly means its people. Only "the world" carries the figure, so "if" and "hates" are dropped from the marked words.
"believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ": "the name" plainly stands for the Son Himself, who is then named. The figure is in "the name", not in "believe in".

"nobody would be saved" is plain English; the Greek "flesh" is not in the BSB words and is not shown.
In "the oath He swore to our father Abraham", "father" is used in its ordinary sense of forefather. No figure is plain here.

After "tell this stone to become bread", the words "Man shall not live on bread alone" read naturally as literal bread. Taking bread for all food is an interpretation, so in doubt it does not go live.
"John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine" reads well as literal bread, given John's set diet. The verse does not plainly show bread standing for all food. In doubt.

places.words_why: In "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see", the eyes plainly stand for the disciples who see. "Blessed are" does not carry the figure.

places.why: "Give us each day our daily bread" makes sense as a plain request for bread. Nothing in the verse shows that "bread" stands for all food or all needs, so the figure is not plain.
"this daughter of Abraham" uses daughter in its common sense of descendant, and here it may also mean a member of Abraham's people. Which one is meant is not plain, so it is in doubt.

"Father Abraham" is the ordinary way to address a forefather, the same as in "Abraham is our father". The verse shows a title, not a plain part-for-whole figure. The marked words also take in the opening quote mark.
"father Abraham" is again the ordinary address to a forefather, not a plainly seen figure. The marked words also take in "No,", which has nothing to do with the figure.
"Jesus, Son of David" is a title, with son in its ordinary sense of descendant. The verse does not plainly show a part-for-whole figure.
"Son of David, have mercy on me!" repeats the title from 18:38. Son means descendant in its ordinary sense, so no figure plainly shows.
"this man too is a son of Abraham" may mean descent, or belonging to Abraham's people even though he is a tax collector. Which one is meant is not plain, so it is in doubt.
"the Christ is the Son of David" quotes the Messiah's title, with son meaning descendant. The verse is about the title, not a plainly seen part-for-whole figure.
"in the breaking of the bread" looks back to 24:30, where He really took the bread and broke it. It names that act, not a meal by one of its parts.
"Peace be with you" is a plain greeting. No part is put for a whole.
"Abraham is our father" uses father in its ordinary sense of forefather, and Jesus goes on to dispute that very claim. No figure is plain.
"our father Abraham" is the ordinary word for a forefather. No part is put for a whole.
"come in and go out and find pasture" carries on the gate and sheep picture of "I am the gate". Reading it as a part for the whole of life takes a commentary.
"Peace I leave with you" promises peace itself. No part is put for a whole.

πάσης σαρκός, "all flesh" for "all people", is a real figure, but it shows only in the Greek. The G3956 tag also lights πᾶν (word 7, "all" You have given), which has nothing to do with it, and the tags cannot be narrowed. Stripping them leaves only "all people", which shows no figure, so the place stays out.

The marked BSB words "about three thousand" are only a number. The BSB does not translate "psuchai" (souls), so the lit words do not carry a part for the whole, and no trim can fix that. "Soul" meaning a person is also an ordinary sense of the Greek word.
"to the breaking of bread and to prayer" uses a set name for a practice. Whether it means a meal or the Lord's Supper is read in by interpreters, so the figure is not plain.
"to break bread from house to house" is a common idiom for eating together. A part put for the whole is not plain without a commentary, and some read it as the Lord's Supper.
"our father David" is the ordinary use of father for forefather. No part is put for a whole.
"our father Abraham" uses father in its common sense of forefather. No figure is plain.
"seventy-five in all" is a count. The BSB does not render "psuchais" (souls), so the marked English words show no figure, and trimming would leave nothing that does.

"Your blood be on your own heads!" is a set saying about guilt. "Heads" could be a part put for the persons, or a picture of guilt coming down on someone's head. It depends on how it is read, so it is not plain enough to go live.
"broke bread, and ate" lists breaking the bread as its own act beside eating, so it is not plainly the whole meal named by a part.
"276 of us" is a number. The BSB leaves out "psuchai" (souls), so the marked English words do not carry the figure, and a trim cannot fix that.

In ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ἀνθρώπου, "upon every soul of man" who works evil, the one who works evil is "man", and distress can fall on the soul itself. So soul for person is not plain, and when in doubt the place stays out.
"our father Abraham" uses father for forefather, as the verse itself explains. No part is put for a whole.
"one man, our father Isaac": Isaac really was the children's father, and "our father" is the ordinary word for a forefather. No figure is plain.

places.words_why: In "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!", the feet plainly stand for the messengers who come. "beautiful are" does not carry the figure.

"a few people, only eight souls" glosses itself: "souls" plainly stands for whole persons. The marked words were the whole verse, so they are narrowed to "eight souls". The tag on psuchai is the right word.
"Peace to all of you who are in Christ" is a closing blessing that means what it says. No part is put for a whole.
"Grace and peace be multiplied to you" is a greeting. The verse shows no plain synecdoche.

"Peace to you" is a short farewell. No figure is plainly shown.

"Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was" is a greeting. No part is plainly named for a whole.

"every eye will see Him" plainly names the eye for the whole person, and the next words speak of the people themselves ("even those who pierced Him"). The figure sits in "every eye", so the span is narrowed to those words.

Listed as cargo, "souls of men" plainly means human persons who are sold: a part for the whole. The marked words were the whole cargo list, so they are narrowed to "souls of men". The tag on psuchas is right.

"Abel was a keeper of sheep, while Cain was a tiller of the soil" plainly sets the two brothers side by side, just before their offerings. The span stopped at "Cain", so it is widened to take in his half.
Abram in Canaan and Lot toward Sodom are plainly set side by side, and 13:13 sharpens it. The span cut off Lot's half, so it is widened.
Isaac and Rebekah are plainly set side by side by the son each loved, after 25:27 sets the sons apart. The span started at "Esau" and left out Isaac, so it now takes in both parents.
"Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was shapely and beautiful" plainly sets the sisters side by side. The span ended at "Rachel", so it is widened to what is said of her.
Unloved Leah, whose womb is opened, and barren Rachel are plainly set against each other. The span left out "was barren", Rachel's side, so it is widened.
Judah plainly sets Tamar beside himself, and the comparison shows up his failure. The span left out "She is", one of the two people, so it is widened.
Orpah's goodbye and Ruth's clinging plainly set the two daughters-in-law side by side. The span left out "clung to her", so it is widened.
Saul plainly sets David beside himself: good repaid against evil repaid. The span left out "You are" and the good and evil clause that carries the contrast, so it is widened.
Martha going out and Mary staying at home plainly set the two sisters side by side. The span left out "stayed at home", so it is widened.

"Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" plainly sets opposites together (loved and hated). Verse 9:12 says the choice was "not by works", so it is not a contrast in which each man's character shows up the other. Antithesis fits, and the span is widened to take in "I hated".
